what: Switzerland votes on plan to cap population at 10 million

clean_source_blocks.text: Can a country put a fixed limit on its population? That is the question Switzerland will be answering on Sunday when voters go the polls to decide on a proposal to cap their population at 10 million, a move that has exposed divisions about immigration in the Alpine nation. The move is backed by the right-wing Swiss People's Party, which describes it as a "sustainability initiative" aimed at easing pressure on housing, public services and the environment. However some voters see this as the party's latest anti-immigration move. Dubbing it a "chaos initiative", the government, other political parties, business leaders and trade unions argue it will deprive hospitals and hotels of much needed staff, and damage hard-won relations with the European Union, leaving non-EU member Switzerland isolated in a very risky world.

Can a country put a fixed limit on its population? That is the question Switzerland will be answering today when voters go to the polls to decide on a proposal to cap their population at 10 million, a move that has exposed divisions about immigration in the Alpine nation. The move is backed by the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, which describes it as a “sustainability initiative” aimed at easing pressure on housing, public services and the environment. However some voters see this as the party’s latest anti-immigration move. Dubbing it a “chaos initiative”, the government, other political parties, business leaders and trade unions argue it will deprive hospitals and hotels of much needed staff, and damage hard-won relations with the European Union, leaving non-EU member Switzerland isolated in a very risky world.
The right-wing Swiss People's Party calls the plan a "sustainability initiative", but opponents say it is a recipe for chaos.

A poster reading "To break away from Europe at a time like this - No to the SVP Chaos Initiative", featuring images of President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, urging people to vote against the Swiss People's Party (SVP) referendum titled "No to a Switzerland with 10 million inhabitants" photographed in Bern, May 18, 2026. Credit: AP/Christian Beutler GENEVA — Swiss voters will take up an unprecedented proposal to limit Switzerland’s population, part of a longtime push by right-wing leaders to cap the number of foreigners who migrate to the rich and economically vibrant Alpine country. A national vote on whether to cap Switzerland's population at 10 million in coming decades culminates with in-person balloting on Sunday. Swiss democracy gives voters a direct say in policymaking through referendums typically held four times a year.

[Lähde: BBC World]
Can a country put a fixed limit on its population? That is the question Switzerland will be answering on Sunday when voters go the polls to decide on a proposal to cap their population at 10 million, a move that has exposed divisions about immigration in the Alpine nation.

The move is backed by the right-wing Swiss People's Party, which describes it as a "sustainability initiative" aimed at easing pressure on housing, public services and the environment. However some voters see this as the party's latest anti-immigration move.

Dubbing it a "chaos initiative", the government, other political parties, business leaders and trade unions argue it will deprive hospitals and hotels of much needed staff, and damage hard-won relations with the European Union, leaving non-EU member Switzerland isolated in a very risky world.

Switzerland's population has grown rapidly since 2002, when it stood at 7.3 million. Now it is 9.1 million, 27% of whom are Swiss residents who were born abroad.

Switzerland's system of direct democracy means all major decisions are taken via the ballot box. Campaigners simply have to gather 100,000 signatures to ensure a nationwide vote.

Many voters are concerned by overcrowded trains, expensive apartments and rising health costs.

The latest opinion polls indicate this could be a very close vote.

They suggest voters are inching towards a no vote by a wafer thin margin, with 52% opposed - but polls remain divided, with 45% saying they are in favour of the proposal and a significant number of voters still undecided.

Helin Genis and Nils Fiechter have a good deal in common, but their diametrically opposed views on limiting the Swiss population are indicative of the polarised nature of this referendum.

Both are young local politicians from immigrant families. Genis is 31 and Fiechter is 29. Genis's parents are originally from Turkey, while Fiechter's mother is from Canada and he holds dual citizenship.

"We have lost control," complains Fiechter, who represents the Swiss People's Party in canton Bern's parliament. "Unchecked immigration is leading to Switzerland no longer being Switzerland."

He believes Switzerland's problems, which he says include a "housing shortage, gridlocked traffic, overburdened schools and strained social services", are a direct result of immigration.

Genis, who is a Social Democrat elected to Bern city council, dismisses these arguments as scapegoating.

payload.title: Sveitsi äänestää väestökatosta, joka rajaisi asukasluvun 10 miljoonaan
payload.summary: Sveitsiläiset äänestävät ehdotuksesta, joka asettaisi maan väestölle 10 miljoonan enimmäisrajan. Aloite on jakanut mielipiteitä erityisesti maahanmuuton, työvoiman ja EU-suhteiden vuoksi.
payload.content:
Sveitsissä äänestetään sunnuntaina poikkeuksellisesta ehdotuksesta, joka rajoittaisi maan väestön 10 miljoonaan asukkaaseen tulevina vuosikymmeninä. Aloitetta ajaa oikeistolainen Sveitsin kansanpuolue SVP, jonka mukaan kyse on kestävyyteen liittyvästä ratkaisusta asumisen, julkisten palvelujen ja ympäristön paineiden hillitsemiseksi.

## Väestökatto jakaa maahanmuuttokeskustelua

Äänestys koskee kysymystä siitä, voiko maa määrittää väestölleen kiinteän ylärajan. Sveitsissä keskustelu kytkeytyy erityisesti maahanmuuttoon, sillä aloite nähdään osana oikeistolaisten toimijoiden pitkäaikaista pyrkimystä rajoittaa maahan muuttavien ulkomaalaisten määrää.

SVP kuvaa aloitetta kestävyyshankkeeksi. Puolueen mukaan väestönkasvu lisää painetta asuntomarkkinoille, julkisille palveluille ja ympäristölle. Vastustajien mielestä ehdotus on kuitenkin ennen kaikkea uusi maahanmuuton vastainen toimi, joka voisi aiheuttaa laajoja käytännön ongelmia.

## Vastustajat varoittavat työvoimapulasta ja EU-suhteista

Sveitsin hallitus, muut puolueet, yritysjohtajat ja ammattiliitot vastustavat aloitetta. Niiden mukaan väestökatto voisi viedä sairaaloilta ja hotelleilta kipeästi tarvittavaa työvoimaa. Lisäksi vastustajat katsovat, että ehdotus voisi vahingoittaa Sveitsin suhteita Euroopan unioniin.

Sveitsi ei kuulu EU:hun, mutta vastustajien mukaan sen yhteydet Eurooppaan ovat ehdotuksen kannalta keskeinen kysymys. He varoittavat, että väestökatto voisi jättää maan aiempaa eristyneempään asemaan aikana, jota lähdeaineistossa kuvataan kansainvälisesti riskialttiiksi.

## Kansanäänestys on osa Sveitsin päätöksentekoa

Kampanjointi on näkynyt myös katukuvassa. Bernissä 18. toukokuuta kuvatussa vastustajien julisteessa kehotettiin torjumaan SVP:n aloite ja varoitettiin irtautumisesta Euroopasta. Julisteessa viitattiin myös Yhdysvaltain presidentti Donald Trumpiin, Venäjän presidentti Vladimir Putiniin ja Kiinan presidentti Xi Jinpingiin.

Sveitsin suorassa demokratiassa äänestäjillä on keskeinen rooli politiikan linjaamisessa. Kansanäänestyksiä järjestetään tavallisesti neljä kertaa vuodessa, ja väestökattoa koskeva valtakunnallinen äänestys huipentuu sunnuntain lähiäänestykseen.
